hook.support: You know how to close up the shop. The new person doesn’t. Can you write it down so they get it right? That is a procedure.
hook.core: You’ve done the closing shift a hundred times. Now a new starter has to do it alone, from your notes. Will the till get counted? Will the fryer get switched off? A good procedure means the job gets done right, every time, by anyone.
hook.extend: A procedure turns what one experienced worker knows into steps anyone can follow safely. Writing one well means thinking like a beginner: what they need, in what order, and where it can go wrong.

why.support: Clear steps keep people safe. They help the job get done right.
why.core: Workplaces run on procedures. Being able to write one makes you useful fast.
why.extend: Clear procedures cut mistakes, train new staff and protect workplaces. Even surgeons use them.

articles.title: Steps anyone can follow

body.support:
A **procedure** tells you how to do a job the right way. It is a list of **steps**.

Good procedures are written for a beginner. Think about someone who has never done the job.

**A procedure has:**
- a clear title.
- the **equipment** you need.
- safety notes.
- numbered steps.
- how to know it’s done.

**Writing the steps:**
- Start each step with an **action word**. “Switch off the fryer.”.
- Put one action in each step.
- Put the steps in order.
- Put a **warning** before a dangerous step.
- Use short, plain words.
- Add a picture if it helps.
.
**Test it.** Ask someone to follow it. Watch where they get stuck. Fix that step.
body.core:
A **procedure** sets out how to do a job safely and correctly, every time. Workplaces use them to train new staff and to make sure jobs aren’t done differently by every person.

**Write for a beginner.** Imagine someone on their first shift. What do they need to know, and in what order?

**The usual parts:**
- **Title:** the job, clearly named.
- **Purpose:** what it’s for.
- **Equipment:** what you need before you start.
- **Safety:** hazards and protective gear.
- **Steps:** numbered, in order.
- **Finish check:** how you know it’s done right.

**Writing the steps:**
- Start with an **action word**: switch, check, wipe, lock.
- One action per step. Long steps get skipped.
- Be exact: “Set the oven to 180°C”, not “turn the oven up”.
- Put a **warning** *before* the risky step.
- Use headings and white space, so people can find their place.
- Add a photo or simple drawing where words aren’t enough, like which switch to press.
.
**Test it.** Give it to someone who has never done the job. Watch, but don’t help. Every time they stop or ask a question, that step needs fixing.
body.extend:
A **procedure** (or standard operating procedure) documents how a task is done safely and consistently. It turns one experienced worker’s knowledge into steps anyone can follow, which is why workplaces use them for training, quality and safety.

**Audience first.** Write for the least experienced person who might use it. Experts skip steps they no longer notice. Beginners need them all.

**Typical structure:**
- **title** naming the task.
- **purpose** and **scope** (who and what it covers).
- **equipment** and materials.
- **safety:** hazards, protective gear, warnings.
- **numbered steps** in time order.
- **finish check** and sign-off.

**Language features:**
- imperatives (command verbs) at the start of each step: switch, check, lock.
- one action per step.
- precise measures: times, temperatures, quantities.
- warnings placed *before* the hazard, often marked visually.
- headings, numbering and white space, so readers can find their place mid-task.
- visuals (photos, labelled drawings) where words alone are unclear.

**Test and revise.** Ask a new user to follow it without help. Each hesitation or question shows a step to rewrite. Procedures should also be reviewed when equipment or rules change.

caseStudies.title: A checklist that saved lives

body.support:
Surgery is risky. Small mistakes can kill.

In **2007 and 2008**, the World Health Organization tested a **checklist** for surgery. It had **19** steps. Teams checked things like the patient’s name and the right part of the body.

Eight hospitals around the world used it. Doctors studied **7,688** patients.

Before the checklist, **1.5%** of patients died after surgery. After it, **0.8%** died. Problems after surgery also went down.

The checklist was simple. But it made sure nobody skipped a step.
body.core:
Surgery is fast and complex. Even expert teams can skip a step. They might forget to check for an allergy.

In **2007–2008**, the World Health Organization tested a **19-item Surgical Safety Checklist** in **eight hospitals** around the world, from London to Manila. Teams used it at three times. Before the patient was put to sleep. Before the first cut. And before the patient left the room.

Researchers studied **7,688 patients**, before and after the checklist. The results came out in 2009:
- deaths fell from **1.5%** to **0.8%**.
- serious complications fell from **11%** to **7%**.

The steps weren’t new. Most teams already knew them. The checklist just made sure they happened, every time.
body.extend:
Modern surgery depends on many people doing many things in the right order. Even expert teams occasionally miss a step.

In **2007–2008**, the World Health Organization trialled a **19-item Surgical Safety Checklist** in **eight hospitals** in eight cities, in rich and poor countries. It was organised around three pauses: before anaesthesia, before the first cut, and before the patient left the operating room.

Researchers compared **7,688 patients** before and after the checklist. Their 2009 results showed:
- deaths fell from **1.5%** to **0.8%**.
- major complications fell from **11%** to **7%**.

The study used a before-and-after design, so other changes over time may have played a part. Still, the result was striking for a one-page document.

The checklist added no new medical knowledge. It worked because of its design: short, ordered, spoken aloud, and placed at the moments when mistakes happen. That is what a good procedure does.

source.name: Harvard Gazette — “Surgical safety checklist drops deaths and complications by more than one-third” (2009)

model.text:
**PROCEDURE: CLOSING THE FRYER**
**Purpose:** Shut down the fryer safely at the end of the shift.
**Equipment:** Heat-proof gloves. Fryer lid.
**Warning:** Oil stays hot for hours. Never move the fryer while it is hot.
1. Switch off the fryer at the wall.
2. Put on the heat-proof gloves.
3. Lift the baskets out and hang them on the hooks.
4. Place the lid on the fryer.
5. Leave the oil to cool overnight.
**Finish check:** Fryer off at the wall, lid on, baskets hung up.
why: The warning comes before any step where you could get burnt.
Each step starts with an action word and has one action.
The finish check tells the worker how to know the job is done.

teacher.overview: Students learn the structure and language of procedures (title, purpose, equipment, safety, numbered steps, finish check; action words first, one action per step, exact details, warnings before the hazard), write a procedure for a real workplace task, and test it on a new user. The case study is the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist study (2009), where a 19-item checklist was followed by fewer deaths and complications.
prep: Collect a few real procedures (school science lab, canteen, workshop) for comparison.
Plan for testing: pairs swap procedures, or test with another class.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — What makes a procedure work
steps: **Hook (10 min):** write steps for making toast; a partner follows them literally.
**Sort (15 min):** good step or needs fixing.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Structure and the case
steps: **Plan (15 min):** choose a task; list steps and hazards.

teacher.answers:
**Annotation:** 1 purpose; 2 equipment before you start; 3 warning placed before the hazard; 4 step starting with an action word; 5 exact detail (2 seconds); 6 one action per step; 7 finish check.

**Sort:** good — lock the front door; set the oven to 180°C; unplug the drill before changing the bit. Needs fixing — “sort out the till and lights and stuff” (split into separate exact steps); “the oven might need turning down” (action word and number); “change the bit (unplug it first)” (move the warning before the action).

**Case study:** a 19-item checklist used at three moments in surgery; deaths fell from 1.5% to 0.8% and major complications from 11% to 7% across 7,688 patients in eight hospitals; it worked by making sure known steps weren’t skipped. Extend: the before-and-after design means other changes may have contributed.

resources.label: Harvard Gazette — surgical safety checklist results (2009)
World Health Organization — Surgical Safety Checklist

realityCheck: **The toast hook works.** Partners follow steps literally (“put bread in toaster” before “get bread”). It makes “write for a beginner” obvious.
**Students without jobs:** let them write for a home or school task (cleaning a bike chain, setting up a gaming console, a canteen job).
**Don’t overstate the study.** It was a before-and-after design; the course says so at extend level.
**Works in a real class:** yes. Testing is the part students remember.

levels.support: Aimed at about Years 3–4 reading: shorter article and case study, 6 key words, word bank and a procedure frame.
levels.core: Aimed at about Years 5–6 reading: the standard version with the six parts, step-writing rules and testing.
levels.extend: Aimed at about Year 7 and up: imperatives, purpose and scope, headings for navigation, and study-design critique.
